name: Nara and Heian Japan
summary: Classical Japan under the imperial court, first at Nara and then Heian-kyō (Kyoto). The Heian era saw the birth of kana writing and great literature such as The Tale of Genji.

location.value: Japan, ruled from Nara (710–784) and then Heian-kyō, modern Kyoto (from 794).

terrain.value: Mountainous islands with small fertile plains.

climate.value: Temperate, with monsoon rains and typhoons.

disasters.value: A smallpox epidemic (735–737) killed perhaps a third of the population.

urbanisation.value: Heian-kyō, planned on a grid like Chang’an, became the capital in 794.

disease.value: A smallpox epidemic in 735–737 killed perhaps a quarter to a third of the population.

migration.value: Scholars and monks travelled to Tang China.

economicBase.value: Rice farming on public and later private estates (shōen).

tradeRoutes.value: Official missions to Tang China until 894; trade with Silla and later Song merchants.

wealth.value: No estimate is possible; the court at Heian-kyō was very rich.

moneyAndTax.value: Early copper coins (Wadō kaichin, 708); taxes in rice and cloth.

inequality.value: Court aristocrats and estate owners above peasants.

governmentType.value: Emperors reigned, but real power lay with the Fujiwara clan as regents.

keyRulers.value: Emperor Kammu (moved the capital, 794), Fujiwara no Michinaga (regent, early 11th century).

succession.value: Imperial line, controlled through Fujiwara marriages.

institutions.value: The ritsuryō legal codes copied from Tang China.

stability.value: Peaceful at court; provinces grew lawless later.

eliteConflict.value: The Genpei War (1180–1185) between the Taira and Minamoto.

armyAndTech.value: Provincial warrior bands that became the samurai.

majorWars.value: The Genpei War (1180–1185) between the Taira and Minamoto clans ended the period.

territoryChange.value: Expanded north into Tōhoku against the Emishi peoples.

alliancesRivals.value: Contact with Tang China and Silla; little foreign conflict after 663.

inventions.value: Two Japanese syllabaries, katakana and hiragana, emerged.

scienceEducation.value: A court university and Buddhist schools.

openness.value: Chinese influence declined and a national culture matured.

communicationTransport.value: Roads (the Gokishichidō) with post stations linked the capital to the provinces; boats on the Inland Sea.

religion.value: Buddhism (including the Tendai and Shingon schools, founded in 805–806) and Shinto.

languageWriting.value: Japanese written in kana; Chinese for official texts.

artsArchitecture.value: The Tale of Genji by Murasaki Shikibu; the Byōdō-in temple.

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to the imperial court and its refined culture.

dailyLife.value: Nobles lived in shinden-style mansions with gardens; farmers in thatched huts; rice, fish and vegetables.

neighbours.value: Tang China and Silla, later Song China and Goryeo.

ideasReligions.value: Buddhism spread widely; Pure Land Buddhism became popular in the late Heian period.

riseSignals.value: Nara became the first permanent capital.

peakPeriod.value: The peak of the imperial court around 1000.

declineSignals.value: The rise of warrior clans (the Hōgen and Heiji Disturbances, 1156–1160).

outcome.value: Ended with the Genpei War; the Kamakura shogunate followed.

sources.value: Court chronicles and diaries. Checked against Wikipedia (“Heian period”).

knownFor.label: The Tale of Genji
knownFor.note: Often called the world’s first novel.
